items.text: A weird experiment I've been trying the last few weeks is having Claude take over day-to-day maintenance of our apps. Seeing early signs of life that this might be possible. The setup is straightforward: we have a Slack channel called proj-claude-maintains-apps. In it, Claude Tag runs a bunch of daily routines across iOS, Android, Desktop, web, CLI, and Agent SDK: - Crash fuzzer: open the app in a simulator and tap around to find ways to crash it, then root cause and fix the crashes - Dup unifier: scans the codebase for similar-yet-slightly-divergent abstractions, and puts up PRs to unify them - Dead-code remover: removes statically unreachable code, and adds logging to suspected dead code...

items.title: Grok Bot is a fantastic release
items.text: Grok Bot is a fantastic release.. the UX, the design, the onboarding :chefs-kiss: But I go back and forth on this a lot: Will users (personal and business) want one super agent that holds all the context or sub agents that are designated to do a slice of tasks? If we treat agents as humans, then the Grok Bot design makes a ton of sense. It allows us to compartmentalize tools, context, outcomes for that person’s division. You reach out to that bot for that specific goal that you have in mind. But, if you treat agents as Jarvis, you want a master agent that just gets the job done. It might create and coordinate all the bots (and dare I say the communication/context) that might be needed to do...

items.title: Prompt debt is the new tech debt
items.text: Prompt debt is the new tech debt. With every model update, you should be cutting at least 50% of your prompts. Most AI products have bloated prompts that are making your product quality worse. The typical flow is: model fails at something -> add 10 rules. Tool call fails -> add 10 examples. Output is weird -> add formatting constraints. 3 months later, your system prompt is a novel. Meanwhile the model is way smarter and your micro-managey prompts are turning it into a dumb rules machine.

items.title: The elimination of engineers was one of the wilder hypotheses out there
items.text: The elimination of engineers was one of the wilder hypotheses out there. Just like absurdly wrong. We just gave engineers a power tool that can accelerate the development of whatever we want. Of course their value not only remains critical in that world, but actually goes up in many domains because we can apply engineering to far more work than before. If you’re trying to automate drug discovery, you need engineers. If you’re trying to automate manufacturing, you need engineers. If you’re taking on larger and larger software projects, you need engineers. This will happen in domains beyond engineering too.
